html:
The Stavnsbånd was a law of 1733 that bound Danish peasant men to stay on the estate where they were born, a kind of serfdom. It was abolished in 1788 as part of a wave of land reforms.

The landowners had wanted it to keep workers on their farms and to give them a hold on recruits for the army. Reformers around the young crown prince argued that free farmers with their own land would farm better.

From the 1780s the open fields were split into separate farms and many tenants became owners. A class of independent farmers grew, which later backed the constitution of 1849, the folk high schools and the cooperative dairies. Danes celebrate the reform as a founding moment of their democracy. It came the year before the French Revolution.
